analysis.one_liner: Bans contracts requiring union-covered workers to pay union fees nationwide.
analysis.headline: The National Right-to-Work Act, backed by 129 House Republicans, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on February 12, 2025, and has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites federal labor law so that no worker anywhere in the country can be required to pay dues or fees to a union that represents them, even though the union must still bargain and represent everyone in the workplace. Right-to-work rules already exist in about half the states by state law; this bill would make them the national standard by amending the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act. Supporters frame it as protecting workers' choice not to join a union; unions and their allies say it lets workers get union representation for free, starving unions of the money they need to bargain and making it easier for employers to resist union demands.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in unionized workplaces who don't want to support the union would keep the dues or fees they otherwise owe — often several hundred to over a thousand dollars a year. Employers gain because unions, with less money and fewer members, become weaker bargaining partners and less able to organize new shops. Groups that have long pushed right-to-work rules, including business lobbies, would get a national version of a policy they have won state by state.

how_it_helps.text: It would strike the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act that allow union security agreements — contracts that require employees in a unionized workplace to pay dues or fees to keep their job — and make such requirements illegal nationwide.
It would do the same for workers covered by the Railway Labor Act, which governs airlines and railroads, by deleting the section of that law that allows union shops.
Supporters present the bill as protecting workers who do not want to join or financially support a union, and 129 House members — all Republicans — signed on to it.

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose the dues and fees that fund their legal, negotiating, and organizing operations, and because federal law requires them to represent every worker in the bargaining unit whether or not that worker pays, they would have to do the same work with less money. Workers who benefit from union contracts — higher wages, better benefits, grievance protection — would bear the cost indirectly if their union grows weaker and the contract erodes. Employers would face less disciplined, less uniform bargaining across workplaces.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and workers covered by union contracts

drawbacks.text: Federal law requires unions to bargain for and represent every worker in the covered workplace, including workers who pay nothing. The bill removes the ability to charge those free riders, so unions carry the same legal duties with a smaller budget — the core mechanism by which right-to-work rules weaken union finances.

Weaker unions mean weaker bargaining on wages, benefits, and safety. Right-to-work states have measurably lower union membership and lower average wages for comparable work, which is the main reason labor organizations treat this bill as the single most damaging change to federal labor law possible.

The bill would impose a national rule on states that have chosen to allow union security agreements, overriding state labor policies in states like California and New York where a majority of voters have not adopted right-to-work rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The individual benefit to a fee-refusing worker is real but small and one-sided: they keep the money while still receiving full union representation, because the bill does not let unions limit services to paying members. The collective cost is larger and falls on everyone in unionized workplaces — unions with thinner budgets bargain harder-bargained contracts less effectively, and decades of evidence from right-to-work states show lower wages and weaker union density where this rule applies. For anyone whose job depends on union strength, the bill is a net loss; for employers, a net gain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee in February 2025, and it has not been scheduled for a hearing or a vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC) introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on February 12, 2025, with 68 original co-sponsors listed on the bill text, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day.
It eventually attracted 128 co-sponsors, all Republicans — a majority of the House GOP caucus — but the committee has taken no action on it since referral.
No version of the bill has received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or a companion Senate introduction so far in the 119th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill sits untouched in committee, leaving both unions and the anti-union employers who want them weakened exactly where they started. If it stays buried, unions and the workers who rely on union contracts are the ones better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act and referred it to the House Education and Workforce Committee.

for.name: 128 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill, making it a majority-endorsed measure of the House GOP caucus.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since it was referred in February 2025, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: AFL-CIO and affiliated unions
against.role: National labor federation and its member unions
against.what_they_did: Oppose national right-to-work legislation as the top legislative threat to union membership and funding, and lobby against such bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 129 sponsors and co-sponsors are House Republicans; no Democrat has signed on, and the bill has no Senate sponsor on the record so far.

industries.note: The bill makes union dues and fees unenforceable nationwide while leaving unions' duty to represent every covered worker in place, cutting the money unions need to bargain, police contracts, and organize. Because union strength is what produces the higher wages and benefits in union contracts, union losses in this bill run against the interests of most union-covered workers.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those resisting union organizing
industries.note: Underfunded unions are weaker bargaining partners and less able to organize new workplaces, giving employers more leverage over wages, benefits, and working conditions. The industry's gain comes directly out of workers' collective bargaining power.

industries.industry: Union-covered workers who decline union membership
industries.note: These workers keep hundreds to over a thousand dollars a year in dues or fees while still receiving full union representation the bill leaves intact. Their individual gain is small and comes at their co-workers' collective expense.

analysis.trajectory: A bill that has sat without a hearing or markup in committee for over a year has a narrow path forward, even with 128 co-sponsors. National right-to-work legislation has never passed either chamber, and even if the House acted, the Senate's 53 Republicans would need Democratic votes to reach 60 to break a filibuster. The realistic outlook is that the bill dies quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless committee leadership gives it floor time.
